newsitem.title: INDIA: India says infrastructure investment badly needed.
newsitem.headline: India says infrastructure investment badly needed.

text.p: India on Tuesday called for speedy infrastructure investments to sustain annual economic growth of about seven percent.
The annual Economic Survey for 1996/97 (April-March) presented by the centre-left government in parliament said infrastructure bottlenecks were impeding growth.
Gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to grow at 6.8 percent in 1996/97 compared with 7.1 percent a year earlier.

The six infrastructure industries -- power, coal, steel, crude petroleum, petroleum products and cement -- grew at 3.3 percent between April 1996 and January 1997 compared with 8.6 percent in the year-earlier period.
"The deceleration in the growth rate of infrastructure is mainly due to a decline in crude oil and hydel power generation," the survey said.

Crude oil production declined by 8.8 percent to 26.51 million tonnes between April 1996 and January 1997 compared with growth of 8.7 percent 29.07 million tonnes in the corresponding period a year earlier.

Hydro-electricity production dipped 6.2 percent to 59.2 billion kilowatt-hours (kwh) between April 1996 and January 1997 compared with a drop of 10.9 percent to 63.1 billion kwh in the same period a year earlier.
The government is trying to woo more private investors to create an efficient infrastructure sector.
The Asian Development Bank has pledged a loan of $300 million to support private infrastructure projects through the "development of the long-term debt market".
The survey said in order to mobilise long-term finance, domestic capital markets have to be reformed to create a vibrant bond market.
It said there was a need to reform pension funds and insurance companies to attract private capital.

The survey said a slowdown in telecommunications growth "suggests that the pace of implementation of telecommunication reform needs to be accelerated and its scope widened to include the Deparment of Telecommunications as a service provider".
The survey also called for a resolution of policy "ambiguities" relating to the aviation industry.
It said the better financial performance of state electricity boards (SEBs) was critical for development of the power sector.

"The commercial losses of SEBs which, in absolute terms, were a little over 40 billion rupees ($1.1 billion) in 1991/92, have shot up over a five year period to 109.41 billion rupees ($3.06 billion) in 1996/97," the survey reported.

The implicit power subsidy to farmers and homes is projected to rise to 215.80 billion rupees ($6.03 billion) in 1997/98 from 192.27 billion ($5.37 billion) in the current financial year ending on March 31, it said.
India supplies power to farmers and household consumers at a subsidised rate.

The government is working on a three-pronged strategy -- encouraging more private capital, liberalising policy to facilitate private investment and restructuring state electricity bodies -- to improve electricity generation. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
